newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's TRI eyes 20 percent of fixed lines.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's TRI eyes 20 percent of fixed lines.

text.p: Malaysian telecommunications company Technology Resources Industries Bhd (TRI) said it hopes to snare between 10 and 20 percent of the country's fixed line subscriber base after 1999.

"If it (equal access) happens, can TRI tap 10 to 20 percent of the traffic out there? I don't think it's too unrealistic," said TRI group executive vice president Wan Aishah Wan Hamid in an interview with Reuters on Monday.
Under a current agreement among industry players, equal access will be introduced on January 1, 1999.
Malaysia's privatised telecommunications utility Telekom Malaysia Bhd has a base of around 3.5 million subscribers and almost all of the fixed-line market, analysts said.

TRI operates the nation's largest mobile cellular communications company, Cellular Communications Network Sdn Bhd (Celcom). "We have around 870,000 active subscribers as at the end of January 1997, accounting for around 67 percent share of the market," said Wan Aishah.
However, TRI's expansion plans will also see it become a provider of fixed-line services. It has already laid down around 3,000 kilometres of fibre-optic cables around the country.
Equal access implies that all of Telekom's subscribers will be able to use alternative trunk and international networks offered by its competitors.

Analysts have speculated that the advent of equal access would hurt Telekom's profitability, but would benefit upstart fixed line operators such as TRI and Time Engineering Bhd's subsidiary Time Telecom Sdn Bhd.
The Malaysian telecommunications market has been plagued by negative sentiments over the level of competition from a total of eight mobile and five fixed-line service providers.
Analysts worry that with so many players, and only 3.5 million subscribers, there is not enough of the pie to go around.

TRI's statistics add to this view. At the end of January 1996, Celcom had 650,000 subscribers, accounting for 75 percent of the local market. Then, Celcom was attracting around 20,000 new subscribers per month.
By September, that number had dropped to 14,000 new subscribers per month. By January 1997, Celcom had a total of 870,000 subscribers, but its market share had been slashed to 67 percent.
The main reason for the drop was intense competition from companies such as Binariang Sdn Bhd's Maxis system, and several other digital operators.
Wan Aishah conceded TRI trailed its competitors in marketing when they launched their systems in 1995 and 1996.
"We decided to wait and see what shape and form they took, what packages they offered," she said. "Now we can really take off."

TRI has been the subject of intense market speculation over the past few months that its management structure has been severely dented by the departure of several key executives, most notably, former Celcom chief Rosli Man. Two senior group vice-presidents have also left.
"There will always be clashes of character in an organisation," said Wan Aishah, who played down the significance of the departures. "It would not be a dynamic organisation otherwise."
